title: AS Computer Science – Chapters 1 & 2 Test
instructions: Answer all questions. Show all working for conversions and calculations. Calculators are not permitted.

questions.text: How many **bits** are there in one **nibble**?
questions.explanation: A nibble = 4 bits (half a byte). Two hex digits = one byte.

questions.text: How many **bytes** are in one **KiB (kibibyte)**? Give the exact value.
questions.explanation: 1 KiB = 2¹⁰ = 1024 bytes. A kB (kilobyte, decimal prefix) = 1000 bytes.

questions.text: What is the denary value of the binary number **1011 0101**?
Convert the denary number **206** to 8-bit binary.

answer.text: 1100 1110 (error carried forward accepted for one place-value slip)

questions.text: Convert the binary number **0110 1011** to hexadecimal.

answer.text: 6B — split into nibbles: 0110 = 6, 1011 = B

questions.explanation: Convert each nibble separately. Anything other than 6B loses a mark.

questions.text: The denary value **-37** is stored as an 8-bit **two's complement** number. Which is correct?
A computer uses 8-bit **two's complement**. What is the **lowest** denary value it can represent?
Perform the binary addition **1011 0110 + 0110 1010**. Show the result and state whether an **overflow** occurs.

answer.text: Correct column-by-column addition with carries
Result (8 bits): 0010 0000 / 0x20 (1 carry out of the most significant bit)
Overflow: yes — the sum needs 9 bits, so the result cannot be held in 8 bits (and the sign changes unexpectedly).

questions.explanation: 10110110 (182) + 01101010 (106) = 288, which is greater than 255, so 8 bits overflow.

questions.text: A bitmap image is 400 × 300 pixels with a colour depth of 16 bits. Calculate its file size in **kibibytes (KiB)**. Show your working.
questions.explanation: File size = width × height × colour depth (bits), then divide by 8 for bytes and by 1024 for KiB.

questions.text: Increasing the **sample rate** when digitising sound increases which of the following?

options.text: The number of samples taken per second
The number of bits used per sample

questions.explanation: Sample rate = samples per second (Hz). Sample resolution = number of bits per sample.

questions.text: Explain the difference between **lossy** and **lossless** compression, and give one file type / format used for each.

answer.text: Lossless: the original file can be reconstructed exactly (no data is permanently removed) — e.g. PNG, FLAC, ZIP.
Lossy: data is permanently removed/reduced in a way the user may not notice, so the original can never be fully restored — e.g. JPEG, MP3.
Correct formats named for both types.

questions.explanation: Lossy gives much smaller files but quality is permanently reduced; lossless keeps quality but compresses less.

questions.text: Which network covers a **single building** such as a school?
questions.explanation: A LAN is confined to a small geographical area, usually one site, and is typically owned by the organisation.

questions.text: In a **client–server** network, which statement is true?

options.text: Every computer stores its own copy of all shared files
A central server provides services and data to the clients
All computers have equal responsibility for security

questions.explanation: The server holds shared resources and controls access; clients request those services. Central management improves security but is a single point of failure.

questions.text: State **three** differences between a **LAN** and a **WAN**.

answer.text: Geographical area: LAN is small (one site); WAN covers a large area (countries/global).
Ownership: LAN is usually owned by the organisation; WAN infrastructure is usually owned by third parties / telecoms companies.
Transmission media / cost: LAN uses its own cabling (e.g. Ethernet/UTP, fibre) and is cheaper to run; WAN uses leased lines/satellite/public networks and is more expensive.

questions.explanation: Other valid: error rates (higher on WAN), bandwidth (usually higher on LAN), security (LAN easier to control).

questions.text: Which device forwards data packets **between different networks** using IP addresses?
questions.explanation: A router works at the network layer, reads the destination IP address and chooses the best route to another network.

questions.text: Describe what happens, in order, when a user types **www.example.com** into a browser and presses Enter. Include the role of **DNS**.

answer.text: The browser asks a DNS server to resolve the domain name into an IP address.
The browser sends an HTTP/HTTPS request to that IP address (the web server) and the server responds with the page data.
The data is transferred in packets (TCP), routed across the internet, and the browser renders the HTML/CSS to display the page.

questions.explanation: Chain: DNS lookup → TCP connection → HTTP request → server response → rendering. Mentioning HTTPS/TLS is a bonus.

questions.text: A **star** topology is used for a small school LAN. What is the main **disadvantage**?

options.text: Adding a new device requires the whole network to be shut down
If the central switch fails, the whole network goes down
A single cable break stops all traffic
Each device needs its own internet connection

questions.explanation: In a star topology every device connects to a central hub/switch, which is a single point of failure. C describes a bus topology.

questions.text: Explain what is meant by **packet switching** and give **one** benefit of using it for sending data over a WAN.

answer.text: Data is broken into packets, each with a header containing the destination IP address and sequence number.
Each packet may take a different route and packets are reassembled in order at the destination.
Benefit: if one route fails packets can be re-routed; the network is used efficiently (packets share links).

questions.explanation: Do not just say 'data is split into packets' — the marks are for route independence + reassembly / the advantage.

questions.text: Which technology allows a user to store files on remote servers and access them from any device?
questions.explanation: Cloud storage/computing moves the resource to a third-party server accessed over the internet.

questions.text: Describe **two** security risks of connecting a school network to the internet and **one** way each risk can be reduced.

answer.text: Risk 1: malware/viruses entering the network (email, downloads) — reduced by antivirus software and filtering downloads/attachments.
Risk 2: unauthorised access / hacking — reduced by a firewall, strong passwords and two-factor authentication.

questions.explanation: Each risk needs a named risk + a matching control, otherwise no mark. Firewall blocks unauthorised traffic; it does not remove malware already inside.
